tests.name: methods_agree
tests.title: Three solvers, one answer
tests.what: Solves the handout's problem (K = 15, c_f = 100, c_h = 2, A ~ Unif{1..5}, at most 200 waiting, γ = 0.95) with enumeration over T = 500 periods, value iteration and policy iteration, and compares the three value functions and policies state by state.
tests.how: The three methods are different algorithms for the same optimality equation, so they must agree: enumeration with T = 500 differs from the infinite-horizon solution by at most γ^500 · max V ≈ 3e-8, and value iteration's stopping rule guarantees ‖V − V*‖ ≤ γ·tol/(1 − γ) (Lean: vi_error_bound). The values of policy iteration must have a zero Bellman residual, all policies must coincide, and the optimal policy must be a threshold rule (dispatch once enough customers wait).

tests.name: contraction
tests.title: Value iteration contracts at rate γ
tests.what: Runs value iteration for γ ∈ {0.5, 0.8, 0.95} and records the change ‖V_{n+1} − V_n‖∞ after every iteration, the ratio of successive changes, and the distance of the final iterate from the policy-iteration solution.
tests.how: The Bellman operator is a γ-contraction (Lean: bellman_contraction), so successive changes must shrink by at least the factor γ every iteration (value_succ_sub_bound) and the number of iterations to a tolerance must scale like log(tol)/log(γ). The stopping rule's a-posteriori bound γ·Δ/(1 − γ) must dominate the true error (vi_error_bound). Ratios are only examined while the changes are far above floating-point noise.

tests.name: first_ten_steps
tests.title: The first 10 steps of backward induction, and 10 periods of the optimal policy
tests.what: On a station capped at 30 customers (same costs, K and arrivals as the handout), records the value function and the optimal first action after each of the first 10 backward-induction steps, recomputes the first two steps by hand in exact rational arithmetic, and then follows the optimal policy for 10 periods from an empty station, printing state, action, cost and next state.
tests.how: With one period left no shuttle is worth dispatching (100 + 2·(s − 15)⁺ > 2s for s ≤ 30), so V₁(s) = 2s exactly; V₂ must equal the hand computation; values must grow with the horizon (Lean: value_mono_horizon) and with the queue (value_mono_state); the dispatch threshold must appear and settle as more periods are added. The 10-period trajectory lets one verify each cost and transition by hand (dispatch exactly when the queue reaches the threshold, 15 customers leave, 1-5 arrive).

tests.name: exact_reference
tests.title: Exact rational arithmetic agrees with the floating-point solvers
tests.what: Re-solves four small instances (two arrival values; a non-uniform arrival distribution; deterministic arrivals; the handout's costs on a 20-customer station) by backward induction in exact rational arithmetic, twice: with Python fractions and with the Lean definition that the formal proofs are about (lean/RLVerify/Shuttle.lean, exported to lean/reference/shuttle_reference.json), and compares with enumeration.
tests.how: The floating-point solver must reproduce the exact values to round-off (1e-12) at every horizon and state, and the optimal first actions must coincide. The Lean values are computed by the very definition whose properties are proved, so this ties the Python implementation to the verified model.

tests.name: discount_sweep
tests.title: γ → 0 makes the agent myopic; more foresight dispatches earlier
tests.what: Solves the problem for γ from 0 to 0.99 and records the dispatch threshold and V(0).
tests.how: With γ = 0 only the current period counts, and dispatching (≥ 100) is never cheaper than holding (≤ 2·200 but 100 + 2(s−15) > 2s), so the myopic agent never dispatches and V(s) = 2s exactly. As γ grows, future holding costs weigh more, so the threshold must not increase and V(0) must increase.

tests.name: parameter_sweep
tests.title: Cost parameters move the dispatch threshold the right way
tests.what: Sweeps the dispatch cost c_f, the holding cost c_h and the capacity K one at a time and records the optimal dispatch threshold; also solves the degenerate cases c_f = 0, c_h = 0 and K = 0.
tests.how: A dearer shuttle must not be dispatched earlier (threshold non-decreasing in c_f); dearer waiting must not delay dispatch (threshold non-increasing in c_h). Free shuttles are dispatched as soon as anyone waits, free waiting or a useless (K = 0) shuttle means never dispatching.

tests.name: structure_changes
tests.title: Changing the structure of the problem
tests.what: Solves variants of the model: (a) up to two shuttles per period; (b) holding cost charged at the end of the period instead of right after the dispatch; (c) holding charged before the dispatch; (d) a station cap of 400 instead of 200; (e) deterministic arrivals (always 3).
tests.how: (a) More actions can only lower the optimal cost, and the second shuttle is only used for long queues. (b) Charging c_h·(left + A) instead of c_h·left adds the constant c_h·E[A] per period, so the policy must be identical and every value must shift by exactly c_h·E[A]/(1 − γ) = 120. (c) Charging everyone present costs more, so values rise. (d) Under the optimal policy the queue never approaches 200, so the cap is irrelevant: values must agree to round-off. (e) With deterministic arrivals a single simulated trajectory has no noise, so its discounted cost must equal V(0) to within γ^horizon.

tests.name: simulation
tests.title: Monte Carlo rollouts reproduce the value function
tests.what: Simulates the optimal policy from several starting queues (5000 trajectories of 600 periods each) and compares the average discounted cost with V*(s); also simulates two deliberately worse threshold policies (dispatch at 5 and at 30).
tests.how: V*(s) is defined as the expected discounted cost of the optimal policy, so the sample mean must land within three standard errors (plus the negligible truncation error γ^600·max cost/(1 − γ)). Any other policy must cost at least as much in every state, both in simulation and when evaluated exactly.

tests.name: policy_iteration_improvement
tests.title: Policy iteration improves monotonically and ends at the greedy fixed point
tests.what: Records every policy visited by policy iteration (starting from 'never dispatch' and, separately, from 'always dispatch'), evaluates each exactly and compares consecutive value functions.
tests.how: The policy-improvement theorem (Lean: policy_improvement) says the greedy policy for V^π is at least as good as π in every state, so the sequence of value functions must be pointwise non-increasing, strictly better somewhere at each step, and both starting points must reach the same policy, which must be greedy with respect to its own values.

tests.name: cuda_kernels
tests.title: The CUDA kernels reproduce the solvers
tests.what: Runs the GPU versions of Section 2 (rl/cuda/dp.py: the state grid initialised on the device, one thread per state for the Bellman sweeps with the value function in shared memory, greedy improvement, and one thread per trajectory for Monte Carlo) and compares them with the numpy solvers. On a machine with an NVIDIA GPU this is the full 201-state problem and 100000 simulated trajectories; without one, the same kernels run in Numba's CUDA simulator on a 31-state instance (slow, so the sizes are small).
tests.how: The kernels implement the same equations with a different execution order (per-thread sparse sums, block-wide max reductions), so values must agree to round-off, policies and iteration counts must coincide, and the per-trajectory simulation must land within three standard errors of V*. The recorded kernel times are real only on a GPU.
